title: Two knights against a pawn
summary: Two knights alone cannot force mate, but against a pawn they can: the Troitsky line, the blockade and the moment to let the pawn go.
part.pawnHelps.title: The pawn that helps
part.pawnHelps.summary: Why one extra pawn for Black makes the mate possible.
part.zugzwang.title: Troitsky's position
part.zugzwang.summary: A mutual zugzwang: whoever has to move loses, whoever can wait draws.
part.line.title: The Troitsky line
part.line.summary: Where to blockade the pawn, and why you never take it.
part.drive.title: The king to the corner
part.drive.summary: One knight holds the pawn; the king and the other knight drive the black king to the corner.
part.release.title: Releasing the blockade
part.release.summary: When to let the pawn go: the mate must come before it promotes.

part.defense.summary: Getting the pawn past the line before the blockade, and the fifty-move rule.

step.t_help: White to move. King on f7, knights on f5 and d2, and the black king stuck on h7. The d2 knight is holding the pawn on d3. How does White deliver mate?
step.t_help.hint1: Imagine the same position without the black pawn. What happens when the black king runs out of squares and nobody is giving check?
step.t_help.hint2: The d2 knight has a better job than watching the pawn. Let the pawn go: every move it makes is a move the black king does not have to make.
step.noPawn: Take the black pawn away and look again. King and two knights cannot force mate against a bare king: when the black king runs out of squares there is almost never a check, and it is stalemate. With the black king on h8 and one of your knights on f6, for example, it would have no move at all. Without the pawn this position is a draw. The black pawn changes everything, because it gives Black something to move when the king cannot.
step.d_help: Watch the black pawn working for White.
step.d_help.m1: Ne4. The d2 knight lets go of the pawn and heads for f6. This and Nf3 are the only winning moves.
step.d_help.m2: Black pushes the pawn. Kh8 does not save it either.
step.d_help.m3: Nf6+. The black king only has h8.
step.d_help.m5: Ne7! Now the black king has no square at all. Without the pawn, this would be stalemate.
step.d_help.m6: But the pawn is there, and Black has to move it. Promoting does not help.
step.d_help.m7: Ng6, mate. The pawn gave Black the one move they needed not to be stalemated.
step.helpMove: Now you, on the other side of the board. It is the same idea mirrored: the e2 knight lets the pawn go and comes in with check, the other one takes the last square, and the pawn does the rest.
step.helpMove.hint: The e2 knight goes to d4 and from there checks on c6. Then the c5 knight goes to d7, and the black king has no squares.
step.helpMove.done: Mate. You let the pawn go on purpose, and its move is what prevented stalemate.
step.t_zz: This is Troitsky's most famous position. White to move: does White win? And if it were Black's turn, what would change?
step.t_zz.hint1: Compare it with the position at the start of the lesson. Which black move takes the black king back there?
step.t_zz.hint2: Think about whether White can pass the move. A knight that leaves a square and comes back to it always spends an even number of moves.
step.zzWhy: It is a mutual zugzwang: whoever has the move is worse off. If Black moves, the only move is Kh7, and we get the position from the start: Ne4, d2, Nf6+, Kh8, Ne7 and Ng6 mate. If White moves, it is a draw: White cannot pass the move. A knight cannot lose a tempo, and the white king finds no route that hands the move back to Black without freeing the black king. Troitsky showed that in these endings the move makes all the difference.
step.d_zzDraw: Now you are Black. White tries everything with the king; watch how the black king defends.
step.d_zzDraw.m1: Kf6. The white king tries another way.
step.d_zzDraw.m5: Kg6. Now the white king watches h7 and g7.
step.d_zzDraw.m7: Ng7. The knight watches e8 and h5.
step.d_zzDraw.m9: Kf6, closing the black king in from the front.
step.d_zzDraw.m12: Kh7! The only move. After Kh8?, White would play Kg6 and Black, to move, would lose. With the king on h7, White cannot repeat the trick, and it is a draw.
step.zzMove: Black went wrong: instead of Kh7, they played Kh8. Now it is your move. Put Black in zugzwang and finish the job.
step.zzMove.hint: The white king goes to g6: the black king will only have g8. Then the d2 knight lets the pawn go and heads for e4.
step.zzMove.done: That's it. Kg6 and Ne4 were the only winning moves. The rest is the pattern you already know: the pawn moves, and the knights deliver mate.
step.t_line: White to move. The black king is in the corner, but there is no net yet, and the pawn on g6 is free. What is White's first job?
step.t_line.hint1: Forget the black king for a moment. Look only at the pawn.
step.t_line.hint2: If the pawn reaches g5, g4 and beyond, can you still hold it and mate in time? Where does it have to be stopped?
step.lineWhy: Ng5! was the only winning move. The knight stops the pawn on g6, and g6 is one of the squares of the Troitsky line: a4, b6, c5, d4, e4, f5, g6 and h4. His rule: if a knight blockades the pawn on this line, or behind it, White wins wherever the kings are (sometimes in more than fifty moves, as you will see). The reason is time. While the pawn is stuck, White drives the black king calmly; when the pawn is released, it still needs several moves to promote, and the mate comes first. Notice the line is not straight: on the b- and g-files it sits further back, on b6 and g6.
step.dontTake: Now a temptation. The f4 knight can take the pawn on g6. Don't! Nxg6 is an immediate draw: without the pawn Black always has a move, and two knights cannot force mate. The black pawn is your ally. Lock it up and keep it alive.
step.lineMove: White to move. The pawn on f5 is on the line, but nobody is blockading it. Stop it now, before it gets past.
step.lineMove.hint: The square in front of the pawn is f4. Which knight gets there, and with what bonus?
step.lineMove.done: Nf4+! The knight blockades the pawn on the line and gives check as well. It was the only winning move: without it, the pawn would cross the line with ...f4.
step.t_drive: White to move. The g5 knight already blockades the pawn on g6, on the line. The black king is on g8. What is the plan? Who works and who stays put?
step.t_drive.hint1: The g5 knight does not need to leave yet. Which squares near the black king is it already watching?
step.t_drive.hint2: The white king and the e4 knight do the pushing. The black king's destination is the h8 corner.
step.driveWhy: The g5 knight does two jobs at once: it holds the pawn and watches f7 and h7, two important squares near the corner. That is why it stays put. The white king and the other knight drive the black king to h8. Only at the end, with the black king caught, does the g5 knight leave.
step.d_drive: Watch the king and the free knight working together. The g5 knight does not move.
step.d_drive.m1: Kf6. The white king takes e7, f7 and g7.
step.d_drive.m2: Kf8. The black king looks for a way out through the centre.
step.d_drive.m3: Nd6. The knight takes e8 and f7: the black king only has g8.
step.d_drive.m5: Ke7. The white king takes f8 and f7.
step.d_drive.m6: Kg7. The black king uses the square the white king left.
step.d_drive.m7: Ndf7. Now h8 and h6 are covered, and the black king only has g8.
step.d_drive.m9: Ne5. The knight goes round to reach g4.
step.d_drive.m10: Kh8. The black king is already in the corner.
step.d_drive.m11: Ng4. From here the knight watches f6 and h6. The black king is left with a tiny corner: g7, g8 and h8.
step.d_drive.m12: Kg7. The net is ready. In the next part, the moment to let the pawn go.
step.driveMove: Now you. It is the same position mirrored: the b5 knight holds the pawn on b6, and the black king is on b8. Drive it to the corner with the king and the d4 knight.
step.driveMove.hint: First the king goes to c6. Then the d4 knight goes to e6, taking c7 and d8.
step.driveMove.done: Well done. The b5 knight never moved: it held the pawn and watched a7 and c7 while the king and the other knight did the pushing.
step.t_release: White to move. The black king is caught between g7, g8 and h8. The g5 knight is still holding the pawn. Is it time to let it go? Find the winning sequence.
step.t_release.hint1: Count the moves the pawn needs to reach g1 once it is free.
step.t_release.hint2: The g5 knight can leave with check. Where does the black king go after that?
step.releaseWhy: Now is the time. The g5 knight leaves with check and releases the pawn. The pawn needs five moves to reach g1, and White needs far fewer to mate. And the pawn's moves are exactly what prevents stalemate: while the black king has no squares, Black moves the pawn. The rule: release the blockade when the black king is already in the net and the mate comes before the promotion.
step.d_release: Horwitz and Kling published this position in 1851. The pawn is on d4, on the line, held by the d3 knight. Watch when and how White lets it go.
step.d_release.m1: Ne2. The g1 knight comes closer and takes c1. Nf3 and Nh3 also win.
step.d_release.m3: Nb4! The blockading knight leaves, and the pawn is free.
step.d_release.m4: Kb1. Black could also move the pawn.
step.d_release.m5: Nc2. The knight comes back and takes a1. The black king has no square: only the pawn can move.
step.d_release.m7: Na3+. The black king goes to a1.
step.d_release.m9: Nc3. Again the black king has no squares, and again the pawn has to move.
step.d_release.m11: Nc2, mate. The pawn gave Black two moves, and both only served to avoid stalemate.
step.releaseMove: Back to our position. Now it is you: release the pawn with check and mate before it promotes.
step.releaseMove.hint: The g5 knight goes to e6 with check. Then the king goes to f7 and the g4 knight to f6.
step.releaseMove.done: Mate, and the pawn never got near g1. Releasing the blockade at the right moment is half of this ending.
step.t_def: Now you are Black. The pawn is on f5, on the line, and the g2 knight is threatening to go to f4. How do you save the game?
step.t_def.hint1: If the knight reaches f4, the pawn is stuck on the Troitsky line. Is there a way to prevent it?
step.pastLine: Black's defence is the other side of Troitsky's rule. Here the pawn is already on d3, past the line. Even blockaded on d2, and with the black king in the corner, it is a draw: the black king is not caught in a net yet, and when the knight lets the pawn go, it reaches d1 too soon. You saw in Troitsky's position that, with the black king already in the net, even a pawn on d3 can lose. So Black is in a double hurry: get the pawn past the line and keep the king out of the net.
step.fifty: And there is the fifty-move rule. Here the pawn is on e4, on the line, still free, and only Ne3, which blockades it, keeps the win. But White wins only without the rule: the first pawn move or capture would come after some sixty-seven moves, and the rule ends the game before that. The longest mate in this ending takes more than a hundred moves. In practice it helps a lot to have the pawn stuck well behind the line, or the black king already near the corner.
step.defMove: Black to move. Save the game.
step.defMove.hint: Do not wait for the knight to reach f4. Use the pawn.
step.defMove.done: f4! The pawn crosses the line before the blockade, and it is a draw. It was the only move: after any king move, Nf4 locks the pawn and White wins.
step.rules: Three rules for your games. One: blockade the pawn with a knight on the Troitsky line, or behind it, and never take it. Two: the blockading knight stays put; the king and the other knight drive the black king to the corner. Three: release the blockade only when the mate comes before the promotion, because the pawn's moves are what prevent stalemate. And count your fifty moves.
step.karpov: Even champions get lost here. In 2000, in the Amber rapid tournament in Monte Carlo, Karpov had a pawn against Topalov's two knights, and the pawn was already past the line. It was a draw, but Karpov went to the wrong corner. This is the position after 74.Ne2: with Black to move, both moves lose, and Karpov resigned.
step.playIntro: Now the whole mate. The pawn on g6 is on the line but not yet blockaded. Lock it up, take the black king to the corner, release the pawn at the right moment and mate. The machine defends as well as it can.
ex.e07: White to move and win. The pawn on a3 is free and racing to a1. Is there time to mate?
ex.e07.hint: Do not give check. A king move leaves the black king with no squares.
ex.e07.solution: Kf7! It was the only winning move. The black king has no squares and only the pawn can move: ...a2. Then Ne5 (Nf6 also works), and after ...a1=Q, Neg6 is mate. The pawn is fast, but the mate is faster.
ex.e09: White to move and win. The black king is caught on h6, but the pawn can still run. Find the three moves that keep the win.
ex.e09.hint: First take the black king's squares, so that Black has to move the pawn. Then stop the pawn again, even past the line.
ex.e09.solution: Ndf6! takes h5, h7 and g8, and Black has to play ...g5. The pawn has crossed the line, but the black king is already caught: Ng3! waits for the pawn, and after ...g4 it is blockaded again. Finally Nfe4!, the only winning move: the knight heads for g5 to close the net, while the g3 knight holds the pawn.
key.help: Two knights alone can't mate, but here the black pawn helps: since Black can still move it, there's no stalemate, and the mate comes.
key.troitsky: A two-way zugzwang: if White is to move, it's a draw; if Black is to move, Black loses.
key.line: The black pawn is held by a knight on a square of the Troitsky line. If the blockade happens no further than this line, White wins.
key.horwitzKling: The knight that was holding the pawn lets it go at the right moment: the pawn's moves avoid stalemate while the other white pieces build the mate.
key.karpov: Topalov against Karpov, Monte Carlo, 2000, a rapid game: Karpov let the draw slip, and here, with Black to move, there is no defence left.
history: Two knights and a king cannot force mate against a lone king: at the last moment there is always a stalemate. The odd thing is that if the opponent still has a pawn, mate can become possible again: the pawn gives Black moves to make, and the stalemate disappears. It's an ending full of surprises that baffles even strong players. The man who unravelled it was the Russian Alexey Troitsky, one of the greatest study composers in history, who worked on it for decades and published his analysis in 1937; years later it turned out to be astonishingly accurate. Troitsky starved to death in 1942, during the siege of Leningrad. Even Anatoly Karpov stumbled here: in 2000, in a rapid game in Monte Carlo, he lost a drawn position to Veselin Topalov.
practice: Now the real ending: the pawn still on g7, free, and the black king on g8. Lock the pawn up, take the king to the corner and release the blockade at the right moment.
ex.e12: Black to move and draw. Topalov–Karpov, Monte Carlo 2000. The pawn on g4 is already past the line, but the g3 knight holds it. With the pawn past the line, the mate only works in some corners. Where does the black king go?
ex.e12.hint: The g3 knight is far from the a1 corner. Think about which corner White can close the net in before the pawn moves, and stay away from it.
ex.e12.solution: Kd2! (Kd1 also holds). The black king stays in the middle of the board, on the pawn's side, and White cannot push it into a corner where the mate comes in time. Karpov played Kb2, heading for the a1 corner, and lost: there the white king and the d4 knight build the net, and the g3 knight only lets the pawn go when the mate comes before promotion.
ex.e11: Black to move and win. Wang Yue–Anand, Nice 2009, a blindfold game. Now Black has the knights, and the white pawn on c3 is about to move. How do you stop it in a way that wins?
ex.e11.hint: To win, the pawn must be held by a knight, on the Troitsky line or behind it. For a white pawn on the c-file, the line runs through c4.
ex.e11.solution: Ne4! The knight heads for c5: after c4, Nc5! locks the pawn on the line, and from there Black wins. Nd2 also wins. Anand played Kc5 and blockaded the pawn with the king, the wrong piece: the win slipped away and the game was drawn. Ne5 would only win without the fifty-move rule.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Study by Horwitz and Kling, 1851. Black has two pawns, the h2 pawn is one step from promoting and the black king attacks the f3 knight. Find the way out.
ex.e14.hint: Remember why the pawn helps: it prevents stalemate. One pawn is enough for that. Then the white king traps the black king in the corner.
ex.e14.solution: Nxh2!! Kxh2. This time taking is right: the h3 pawn stays on the board, and it is enough to prevent stalemate. Kf1! Kh1 Kf2 Kh2 Ne3 Kh1 Nf1 h2 and Ng3 is mate: the pawn on h2 blocks its own king's escape. The study starts earlier, with 1.Ngh4+ Kg1 2.Nf3+ Kh1 3.Ke1 Kg2.
ex.e13: White to move and win. Study by Chéron, 1955. The pawn on g3 is already past the line, but the g2 knight holds it and the black king is caught in the corner. If it were Black's move, the mate would come quickly. Make it Black's move.
ex.e13.hint: A king does not lose a move by going back and forth. It needs a path of three squares around c2, without letting the black king out of the corner.
ex.e13.solution: Kc3! Kb1 Kd2! Ka1 Kc1! Ka2 Kc2! The white king walked a triangle (c3, d2, c1) and came back to c2: the position is the same, now with Black to move. Kd3 on the third move also works. From there the white king goes to b3, the c4 knight closes the net and the g2 knight lets the pawn go only when the mate comes before promotion. Chéron showed that, with the black king already caught, not even a pawn well past the line saves Black.
